replies.author: Dead_Fox_7
replies.body:
Part of this I dipped into seedream 5.  1.) found a character at the beginning with the proportions I wanted (larger head, smaller body, correct side angle, etc. 2.) Traced that in a simple basic outline in photoshop. 3.) Took that outline to Seedream 5 and asked for a forward front and back shot next to the side angle 3.) Fed that outline along with any character I wanted into Grok with a basic prompt of 'make the character in image 2 the angle (side, front, back) and proportions of the outline in image 1.  4.) isolated each of those new 3 shots (side, front, back) on a 1:1 black background (i find that black backgrounds work best when you need to remove backgrounds later as it doesn't leave faint ghosted pixels and helps pop the edges) 5.) brought those three now separate images into Grok with a simple 'Walking in place animation' and would expand on that if needed (looping, fluid animation, arms at side, whatever it is you're looking for that the initial generations aren't giving. 6. Bring that video into Premiere and isolate the loop (many times it's about 1 second long found within the 6 sec clip) 7.) Bring into any app that lets you extract frames to make a sprite sheet (I used sorceress.games) 

bonus: one you have just one good looping animation? Kling O1 video edits has proven to be incredibly nice in transferring motion to another character 'Replace the character in Video 1 with the character in image 2'. All the characters you see in game are based off just one good animation set from the steps above. 

Hope that helps!

replies.author: Dead_Fox_7
replies.body: Custom. But the only reason I went that route is because Claude recommended it and not through any cleverness on my part. I laid out what I was looking to achieve and it recommended python/pygame. Since my background is illustration, who was I to know any better?

replies.author: StrategySilent9360
replies.body: Can you elaborate on what custom means?

replies.author: Dead_Fox_7
replies.body:
Sure. Just know my knowledge and terminology is pretty basic in this area. After discussing with Claude and letting it know that I have zero coding knowledge, it recommended using python/pygame that it would use to make the game engine itself. When I initially thought game engine my first thought was that it was going to attempt to build some monstrosity like Unreal 6 but 2d. It's not that at all. It's just been Claude plugging in sprites when it needs to, establishing how they move and interact with the world, etc.

Honest advice? Just be straight with Claude and say 'I have no idea where to even begin with 'x' or 'y'' and ask for options and what it recommends. That in itself saved me a LOT of time. Then feel free to verify against other models and get a second opinion

comments.author: Mecanos3
comments.body: How did you set up the images? Did Claude create everything instantly? I'm currently developing a strategic survival game, but I'm having a lot of trouble finding the right sprite sheets/image assets. Any advice?

replies.author: Dead_Fox_7
replies.body: Claude just did the coding. Grok mainly did the imagery (notable exception were the ground tiles which I did myself) that I would then bring into photoshop to tie in to the other images. I used grok for the animations, Premiere to make the looping animations fluid and then [sorceress.games](http://sorceress.games) for the sprite sheets. Sorceress is a paid site, but if you're just pulling sprite sheets I'm sure there's options out there.
